Partial-rollout checkpointing for NeMo Gym and NeMo RL

Design v2 on the environment-server architecture, with the v1 proposal preserved · draft for review

A long agentic rollout should survive a trainer checkpoint and a crash without being thrown away. This page walks through the lifecycle message by message: a normal episode, a checkpoint taken in place, a crash followed by a restore, a straggler that misses the deadline, and a generation that is cut mid-decode. Each step shows who sends what to whom and what every component's state machine is doing.

Part 1

The problem

Why checkpoint rollouts that are still running

Reinforcement-learning training periodically checkpoints the trainer so it can survive a crash or a preemption. Agentic rollouts make that hard: a multi-turn rollout with tool calls, a software-engineering task, or a long judged conversation can run for minutes or hours, and thousands run at once. There are two simple answers, and both fail at scale:

  • Restart every unfinished rollout after a crash. Every token already generated and every tool call already run is thrown away, and long rollouts may never finish between failures.
  • Wait for every rollout to finish before checkpointing. Checkpoint latency becomes the latency of the slowest rollout, and one hung tool call or harness blocks the checkpoint indefinitely.

Partial-rollout checkpointing takes a consistent snapshot while rollouts are in flight, then continues each one from its last safe point after a crash, without repeating work that has side effects and without waiting for stragglers.

The state a running rollout spreads across

One rollout is not one process. At any moment its state lives in several places:

WhereWhat must survive a crash
Environment server (Gym)Where the episode is in its protocol: which step runs next, which sessions it opened, and the results of steps already done
Agent server (Gym)The turn loop: the conversation so far, tool calls not yet answered, and session cookies
Resources server (Gym)Environment state per session, such as a counter, a database, or a document store that tools change
Policy model server (Gym)The token-free lineage of model calls, and which responses have not been delivered yet
Inference workers (training framework)Generated tokens, including the prefix of a generation still decoding
Training frameworkThe durable token store, the registry of dispatched rollouts, and the global checkpoint itself

Every rollout also has an identity that survives retries and restores: a stable rollout ID plus an attempt number. After a restore the rollout continues as the next attempt, and nothing of an older attempt may still be running anywhere.

What a correct checkpoint requires

  • One consistent cut. Every component's saved state describes the same moment of the same rollout.
  • No repeated side effects. A step that changes state is never run twice because of a restore.
  • Bounded latency. A checkpoint never waits for a generation or a slow rollout to finish; the controller can retire a straggler, which then restarts from its input.
  • Durable before published. Every component's files are complete and verified before the global checkpoint names them.
  • Retired work stops. Retiring an attempt stops its work everywhere before it returns, so nothing from a replaced attempt can still change state.
  • Nothing grows without an end of life. Every piece of state has an owner and an event that frees it; a restart does not count.
  • Fail closed. A server that cannot continue a rollout still takes part, so it can never silently produce a checkpoint that is wrong.

How it fits with NeMo RL

The training framework owns the global checkpoint transaction; Gym owns everything inside Gym.

  1. Prepare. The framework stops dispatching new rollouts, pauses its trainer and trajectory assembler actors until resume, and asks Gym to prepare. Gym brings every in-flight rollout to a safe point, in the order Gym defines, and reports any straggler it had to wait for.
  2. Commit. Gym writes each server's state into the framework's checkpoint directory. The framework saves its own state (token store, rollout registry, dataloader) alongside, and waits for results of rollouts that finished just before the cut.
  3. Publish, then resume. The framework publishes the checkpoint atomically and tells Gym to resume.
  4. Restore after a crash. The framework starts fresh Gym servers, restores Gym's state for the rollouts it will continue, and re-dispatches each of them as its next attempt, which continues from its last safe point.

Part 2 is how v2 does this. Part 3 is the first proposal, kept as it was. Part 4 compares them.

Part 2

The v2 design

What this design does

Training and evaluation runs keep thousands of rollouts in flight at once. When the job crashes or is preempted, every one of those rollouts is lost and has to start over from its input. Some rollouts, such as software engineering tasks, run for tens of minutes, so a single preemption can throw away hours of generation.

This design lets whatever process sends rollouts to Gym save the ones in flight and continue them after a crash. That process is called the controller. Gym does not care which program plays the role: a trainer and an evaluation run use the same calls and get the same guarantees.

Four rules carry the design. Each rollout records a safe point after every step it completes, and a checkpoint saves it at the latest one, so nothing is ever saved halfway through a step. Each run of a rollout carries an attempt number, so after a crash the saved rollout continues as its next attempt and Gym can refuse anything the old attempt still sends. Every Gym server takes part in every checkpoint, and a rollout that touches a server unable to save its state is simply left out: it keeps running, and if a crash does happen it starts over. Finally, Gym checkpoints its servers in a fixed order of its own, so the controller asks for one checkpoint and never sequences servers itself.

In a test deployment on one workstation, 16,000 rollouts with about 12,000 in flight were prepared in 3.6 to 7.6 seconds, written in 1.8 to 4.6 seconds and restored in 3.2 to 5.0 seconds, and every saved rollout finished after the restore.

What the design must guarantee

The requirements are listed in priority order, and when two of them conflict the earlier one wins.

  1. A continued rollout behaves as if it was never interrupted. It sees the same state and continues the same token lineage, and no step runs twice unless that step has been declared safe to repeat. When Gym cannot guarantee this for a rollout, it restarts the rollout from its input instead.
  2. Every piece of checkpoint state has an end of life. Each piece is freed by an explicit event, such as a retire or a later commit, so nothing grows with the length of the run and nothing waits for a restart or a timeout to be cleaned up.
  3. A rollout that cannot be saved never stops the others from being saved.
  4. Checkpoints are fast enough to run often. Tens of thousands of rollouts in flight should take seconds, so checkpoints can run on a timer and right before a preemption.
  5. The design has as few moving parts as the requirements above allow. There is no acknowledgement protocol, no background sweep, and no state shared between servers.
  6. Nothing changes when checkpointing is off. Without a checkpoint: block in the configuration, no server installs any checkpoint route or behavior.

Two things are out of scope. Gym does not support several Gym deployments sharing one policy model, and saving the controller's own state, such as a trainer's, is the controller's job.

Terms used in this design

Later sections use each of these terms only in the sense given here.

ControllerThe process that sends rollouts to Gym and decides when to checkpoint, such as a trainer or an evaluation run.
Rollout and attemptA rollout has a stable ID, and each run of it is an attempt numbered from 0. r-a1 means attempt 1 of rollout r.
ParticipantThe part of one Gym server that owns state a checkpoint must save. The four kinds are environment, policy model, agent and resources.
BoundaryThe safe point an episode records after each step it completes, naming the next step and what that step needs.
Wait step and replay stepA step still running when a checkpoint starts. The checkpoint waits for a wait step to finish, while a replay step simply runs again after a crash, so it must be safe to repeat.
Continue and restartAfter a crash, a saved rollout continues from its boundary as its next attempt, while a rollout that was not saved restarts from its input as its next attempt.
PrepareStops each server from admitting new work and waits until every rollout in flight sits at a boundary, or reports the ones that cannot be saved.
CommitWrites each server's state for the rollouts the controller will continue into the checkpoint directory.
ResumeReopens every server after a checkpoint. It also cancels a checkpoint that was not finished, so it doubles as the abort.
RestoreInstalls a checkpoint's state into fresh server processes after a crash, so each saved rollout can continue as its next attempt.
RetireAbandons an attempt: every server stops its work, frees its state, and from then on refuses its late requests.
ForgetTells every server that a retired rollout is finished for good, so it can drop the entry it kept to refuse that rollout's late requests.

Components and what each owns

Select a component to see what it owns, what it checkpoints, and what it never does.

One checkpoint from start to finish

The controller sends rollouts to environment servers as usual. For checkpoints it calls Gym's coordination functions, which in turn call every participant, so the controller never talks to an individual server.

Rollouts flow through environment servers, and checkpoint calls flow through coordination.

A checkpoint, followed later by a crash, unfolds in five stages:

  1. The controller stops sending rollouts and calls prepare. Each participant stops admitting new work, and each episode in flight finishes its current step if it is a wait step and then stops at its next boundary.
  2. When prepare returns, every participant has reported whether it is ready and has listed the rollouts in flight that it cannot save. Those rollouts are called restarts.
  3. The controller calls commit with the rollouts it will continue, leaving the restarts out, and every participant writes its records followed by a manifest that names them.
  4. The controller saves its own checkpoint, recording which rollouts continue and which restart, and only then calls resume so everything carries on.
  5. If Gym crashes later, fresh Gym processes start and the controller calls restore and then resume. It retires each restart's old attempt and sends every rollout again as its next attempt, so saved rollouts continue where they stopped and restarts begin from their input.

Step through the lifecycle

Pick a scenario and step through it. In the diagram, the current step's messages are drawn at full strength; earlier steps are faded. The boxes under the diagram show each component's state after the step; a thick solid border marks a change and a dashed border marks a problem state. The scenarios use a training framework as the controller; rollout collection plays the same part in evaluation runs.

    State machines in the walkthrough

    Every participant runs the same control-phase machine. Agent sessions, policy calls, and episodes have their own small machines. While a scenario plays, the machine that the current step affects highlights its current state with a thick solid border.

    The state machine every server runs

    Every participant runs the same control code, reached through bearer-protected routes under /ng-control/v1/checkpoint. This shared code, the control plane, tracks which phase the participant is in, which checkpoint is active, how long the controller's lease lasts and how state is written, so each kind of server only has to describe its own state.

    The phases of one participant. Retire and forget are accepted only in idle and restored.

    Rules that keep the phases safe

    Only one checkpoint can be active at a time, and a call naming a different checkpoint ID is refused with checkpoint_conflict. Once a checkpoint has been resumed it can never come back: resume records the checkpoint's ID, so a delayed call from an old controller cannot reopen or overwrite anything. Gym keeps the last 64 resumed IDs, which is enough to catch stale calls while keeping the record small.

    A controller that disappears cannot leave Gym closed either. Every call renews a lease that lasts until the call's deadline plus lease_grace_seconds (600 seconds by default), and when the lease expires the participant resumes on its own, which is the same as cancelling the checkpoint.

    Every finished call can be repeated safely. A repeated commit returns the same reply as the first, so the controller can retry any call with the same checkpoint ID without worrying about what already happened. Before writing anything, commit also checks that the participant is still ready, and fails with invalid_phase if something changed since prepare, so Gym never writes a state that is no longer consistent.

    The order Gym checkpoints servers in

    The order in which servers are prepared, resumed and retired matters for correctness, and it depends on which Gym server calls which, so Gym fixes it rather than leaving it to the controller. The coordination functions keep no state between calls, which lets the controller call and retry them freely.

    CallOrderReason
    prepareEnvironment servers, then the policy model, then agents, then resources servers, each stage ready before the next starts.Environment servers stop their episodes first. The policy model then holds its responses, so agents waiting on it reach a boundary, and resources servers go last because agents keep calling them until they stop.
    resumeThe reverse.No server reopens before the servers it calls.
    commit and restoreAll servers at once.By then every server is stopped at a consistent point, so writing is independent.
    retire and forgetEnvironment servers, then agents, then the policy model and resources servers together.A caller stops before the servers it calls, so nothing upstream sends new work for the attempt.

    None of these calls is atomic across servers

    Each coordination call reaches every server separately, so a call can succeed on some servers and fail on others. What makes this safe is that every call can be repeated with the same ID, and that a partly finished call never produces a state the controller would act on. The table below says what each call leaves behind when it fails partway, and what the controller does about it.

    CallAfter a partial failureWhat the controller does
    prepareSome servers are prepared and others are still preparing, with admission closed on all of them.Calls resume, which reopens every server, and tries again later.
    commitSome servers have written their records and manifest, and others have not. The checkpoint is not valid yet, because the controller has not published it.Repeats the commit, which reuses each server's single write, or resumes without publishing. A directory from a commit that was never published is the controller's to delete along with any other checkpoint it does not keep.
    resumeSome servers are open and others are still closed until their lease expires.Repeats resume. A server that already resumed recognizes the checkpoint ID and returns at once.
    restoreSome servers have installed state and others have not.Nothing: coordination undoes it on its own by retiring the new attempts on every server, which frees what was installed, then resuming every server and reporting the error. The controller starts those rollouts over from their input.
    retireStages run in order, so a failure stops the call: earlier stages have retired the attempt and later stages may still be running its work.Repeats the retire until it succeeds. A server that already finished finds nothing left to stop and returns at once, and the refusal it recorded stays in place either way.
    forgetSome servers have dropped the entry and others still hold it.Repeats the forget. Until then the remaining servers only keep refusing requests that should never come.

    Restore is therefore the only call with built-in undo. Every other call relies on the controller repeating it, and the controller rules require exactly that.

    How episodes are saved

    The environment server runs the episode protocol, so it is the one that records where each episode can continue. The main protocol today, single_agent_turn, runs five stages with one agent and records a boundary before each of them. A protocol with several agents would record boundaries in the same way, with each boundary naming every session it needs.

    StageStep typeReason
    Start the resources and agent sessionsReplayStarting a session with a caller-chosen session ID can safely run twice.
    Run the agentReplayThe agent stops at its own turn boundaries and continues from them.
    Close the agent sessionWaitClosing returns the agent's observations only once.
    VerifyWhatever the resources server reported when its session startedOnly the resources server knows whether its verification can run twice.
    Return the resultBoundary onlyThe result is recorded, so a restore never verifies twice.

    The states of one episode inside the environment server. Time an episode spends stopped for a checkpoint does not count against its deadline.

    Every episode in flight can be saved. An episode that has not reached its first boundary yet is saved with an empty boundary and starts over from its input after a crash, while a restored episode stays at the boundary it was restored from until it records a new one.

    The subtle case is a replay step that ends while a checkpoint is open. The checkpoint has already counted the episode at the boundary before that step, so the step's result must not move the saved boundary. Instead the result waits at the next boundary until resume, and the saved boundary and the episode's real progress never disagree.

    How the policy model avoids waiting

    A generation can take minutes, so the checkpoint never waits for one to finish. This is safe because of a simple fact about agents: an agent waiting for a model response is still at the boundary it recorded before making the call. If the call is made again after a crash, the continued rollout matches its saved state exactly.

    One model call across a checkpoint. A call that arrives while a checkpoint is open waits outside the gate, so prepare never counts it, and its caller is still at the boundary it recorded before the call.

    Calls that have not been delivered are left out

    When admission closes, the model holds every response that has not started streaming, and the checkpoint leaves out those calls together with their rows in the capture ledger. After a crash the agent simply makes the call again. Only a response that is already streaming has to finish before prepare is ready.

    Generation cuts save compute but are never required

    With generation cuts turned on, prepare also asks each inference worker to save the tokens it has generated so far for each held call. After a crash, the repeated call continues from that saved prefix, called a cut, instead of generating it again. Because a cut is only an optimization, a call the worker could not cut is generated again, which is always correct. The cut request gets half of the time left for prepare, so a stuck worker cannot use up the time the later stages need. A call with constrained decoding is never cut and never continues one, since a token prefix cannot restore its structured decoder.

    Some inference backends, such as Megatron inference, take cuts at a different address from their OpenAI API. Each of them lists a generation_cut_control_url, and once those addresses are set, a backend without one fails its cut rather than guessing where to send it.

    Token lineage continues under the next attempt

    Restore imports the capture ledger's rows under the next attempt's capture key, so the repeated call finds its parent through normal fingerprint matching without any extra header.

    A model server restores only into a fresh process

    A model server that has already served a call refuses to restore, because a ledger it wrote might belong to a live episode. With several workers, restore is also refused once any worker has left, since its replacement cannot report what the old worker served.

    Ledger cleanup waits for resume

    The controller removes old capture ledgers through retire and delete routes on the model server. Those routes answer 409 while a checkpoint is open, because commit reads the ledger of every continued rollout.

    How agents are saved

    An agent that implements the session hooks saves each session at its latest turn-loop boundary. Simple Agent, the one Gym ships today, records a boundary before each model call and another after each model response whose tool calls have not run yet. The hooks hand the session's state to the checkpoint and rebuild it after a restore, and they are asynchronous and take every session at once, so an agent that keeps state outside its process can save all of it concurrently.

    The states of one agent session. A session waiting for a model response counts as stopped at its last boundary.

    Whether an agent can be saved depends on whether it implements the hooks, not on how its harness is built. An opaque harness can be saved if it runs in a sandbox that can snapshot its whole runtime, for example one backed by a microVM: the agent's hooks pause the sandbox and save a reference to its snapshot, and after a crash they resume that snapshot. Two pieces of that path are still open, and the known gaps describe them. An agent without hooks is treated as one that cannot be saved, and its rollouts restart.

    When the policy model refuses a call during a checkpoint, Simple Agent stops at its boundary and makes the call again after resume. A legacy /run, where the agent drives the whole episode itself, is tracked as an episode of its own: its session start and turn loop are replay steps, and its verification uses the step type the resources server reported. Finally, each run of a session reports its observations under its own invocation ID, and the session's saved state includes how many runs it has started, so a restored session's next run takes the next ID while a continued run keeps the one it already had.

    How resources servers declare their state

    Each resources server states in its code how its sessions are saved. This is a class attribute rather than a configuration setting, because only the server's author knows whether its state can be saved, and a setting could claim support the code does not have.

    The three modes. A server nobody has reviewed falls back to restarting its rollouts.

    The server learns each session's lifetime from requests it already serves. A successful /seed_session ties the session to the episode named in the request's rollout path, and a /close_session or /verify ends it, so no route has to be labelled as a change or a read.

    Requests already running finish before the server's state is saved: prepare is ready only once nothing is in flight, and a session start in progress counts too, so the saved sessions always match the environment server's boundary. A request that arrives while a checkpoint is open waits for resume instead of being refused. Only a rollout that keeps running through the checkpoint sends such a request, since a rollout that will be continued has already stopped at a boundary, and refusing it would show a tool error to the model in a third-party harness.

    The reply to /seed_session tells the caller two things without another request: x-ng-checkpoint-verify says whether /verify can run twice, and x-ng-checkpoint-restart says the server cannot save this session. Saved state is written exactly as the server holds it, keeping dictionary key order, NaN and infinities, because tool outputs often serialize stored state and a restored session must answer exactly as the original would.

    Rollouts that cannot be saved

    A rollout can only be saved if every server it uses can save its part. When one of them cannot, because it is an agent without session hooks or a resources server in restart_only mode, the rollout is a restart. Earlier versions of this design made a restart block every checkpoint until the controller retired it, which meant one such rollout in flight stopped every other environment in the run from being saved and threw away its own progress at each checkpoint even when nothing crashed. A restart now flows through the checkpoint without stopping anything:

    How a restart is found, reported, left out of the checkpoint, and recovered after a crash.

    The design still fails closed if a controller ignores the restart list. Each participant checks the commit's list against its own restarts and refuses a commit that names one with restart_in_scope, so such a controller gets a failed checkpoint rather than a rollout that is only partly saved.

    The restart list also never changes while a checkpoint is open. An episode is marked as a restart only after any open checkpoint ends, and session starts on servers that cannot save state wait for resume as well. The random sequence tests found why this matters: a session start whose reply arrived in the middle of a checkpoint used to change the list after the state had been written, and the commit then failed.

    After a crash, the retire that comes before the rerun is what protects it. A harness can run in a remote sandbox that survives the crash, and if it kept calling Gym, its calls would mix into the new attempt's data. The retire makes every server refuse them. An environment protocol that records no boundaries at all treats every episode as a restart, which is why nemo_user_sim episodes no longer block checkpoints.

    How Gym abandons an attempt

    The controller abandons an attempt by calling retire, and every participant handles it the same way, callers first. It marks the rollout as retired up to that attempt, stops the attempt's work and waits until that work has ended, frees the attempt's state, and only then replies.

    The entry lasts exactly as long as a late request can still arrive.

    The entry exists because of late requests. A request that a caller sent just before its own retire travels on a different connection than the retire itself, so it can reach a server after that server has already finished retiring the attempt. Without the entry, the server would accept it and write its rows into the capture files. The entry is a single item per rollout that never moves to a lower attempt and survives even a failed retire, and the controller deletes it with forget once nothing of the rollout can still run.

    A retire is refused while a checkpoint is open, because stopping an episode waits for its final cleanup while that cleanup's own calls wait for resume, and the retire would wait forever. To give up on a straggler, the controller therefore resumes first, retires it, and then prepares again. A retire that runs out of time is safe to repeat: the episode stays tracked until its task has ended, blocks the next checkpoint in the meantime, and a second retire waits for it again without cancelling the work twice.

    On the policy model, retiring attempt N also cancels the calls of attempts 0 to N, waits for them, and then retires their capture ledgers in one batch.

    How a checkpoint is written

    Each participant writes one directory per checkpoint, holding a records file and a manifest that names it. The checkpoint counts only once every participant has written its manifest and the controller has published its own checkpoint.

    State is taken once per checkpoint, and resume and publishing share one lock.

    Each checkpoint takes its state once and writes it once. The writing runs in a thread, which a deadline cannot stop, so the control plane keeps hold of that one write: a repeated commit waits for it, and if storing failed, the repeated commit stores the same records again. A checkpoint's saved state therefore can never change between attempts to commit it.

    No manifest can appear after resume has returned. The writer checks a stop flag before each record, and its last check, the rename of its records file and the creation of the manifest all happen under a lock that resume also takes. Two writers can never leave mismatched files either, because the records file is named after its content hash and the manifest is only ever created, never replaced. If two writers race, exactly one publishes and the other removes its own records file.

    Saved state reads back exactly as it was written. Records keep every dictionary's key order, NaN and infinities, and Gym checks opaque state once to confirm it is JSON before writing it unchanged, using orjson for the check and strict JSON as the fallback. A value that would not read back the same fails the commit with an error naming the rollout. Records are encoded, hashed and written one at a time and read back the same way, so neither commit nor restore ever holds a whole records file in memory, and restore keeps only the records it will install while still verifying the whole file.

    How a checkpoint is restored

    Restore runs in fresh processes after a crash. Each participant stops admitting work, reads and verifies its records, and installs the ones the controller continues under the next attempt. It then waits for the controller's resume before admitting any of those attempts, and each restored record stays until its new attempt actually starts.

    Before installing anything, a restore removes what earlier failed runs left behind. Suppose a continued rollout made model calls and Gym crashed again before the next checkpoint: restoring the same checkpoint again deletes everything those runs left for the target attempt and every later attempt, including ledgers, token records and retire fences. A fence left in place would otherwise silently drop the restored rollout's rows. To make this possible, each participant is told every rollout the restore continues, including ones it holds no record of, so a participant that keeps files per rollout can clear them too.

    A restore that runs out of time reopens admission only once its install has finished, and the retire that cleans up a failed restore waits for the install as well. Restored state that no new attempt ever uses is not kept forever: the next checkpoint saves it again for as long as the commit names the rollout, and the first commit that leaves it out deletes it. It deletes it without a fence, because the controller may still start that rollout over as the same attempt.

    Servers with several workers

    Production servers run several uvicorn workers that share one port. A checkpoint call reaches whichever worker accepts the connection, while a session's state lives only in the worker that created it. Two mechanisms make such a server behave as a single participant.

    On the left, one participant for the whole server. On the right, requests reaching the worker that holds their session, with no shared table.

    A coordinator in the server's main process owns the participant. Each worker reports to it over a local socket, and it tells every worker when to close, reopen, retire, save and install. Prepare is ready only once every worker is, and if fewer workers have registered than configured, or a worker is lost while a checkpoint is open, the checkpoint waits until resume, because what that worker held is unknown.

    Session requests find their worker through the owner ID in the signed cookie or MCP token the client already sends, and a request whose owner is gone gets a 410 instead of running against empty state. The number of workers may change between a checkpoint and its restore: restored sessions are placed on live workers, and every router receives a table mapping old owner IDs to new workers, plus one mapping session IDs to workers for sessions saved by a server that had one worker. Every worker's restarts reach the coordinator, which combines them into its own report, so a commit that names any worker's restart is refused.

    Rewards computed over a group

    GenRM comparison scores each rollout against the other rollouts for the same prompt. Each member's /verify waits inside the resources server until the whole group has arrived, and the server then compares them all and answers every member at once. The server is declared stateless with verification that may run twice, because the group lives in memory, keyed by the group ID and group attempt the caller sends, and there is nothing per session to save.

    The checkpoint must not wait for a member's verification, because that verification waits for other members that may still be generating while generation is paused for the checkpoint, and the two would wait for each other forever. A member waiting in verification is therefore saved at the boundary before verification. After a crash, every member that had not recorded its reward verifies again and the group forms again in the new process, provided the controller keeps each group's group attempt unchanged.

    One crash timing is slow but still correct. If Gym crashes just after a group's comparison, when some members have recorded their reward and others have not, the remaining members wait for members that will never verify again. They fail after cohort_collection_timeout_s, 30 minutes by default, and then restart from their input.

    Situations a real run hits

    Each situation below has a test that fails without the behavior described.

    When the controller or a deadline fails

    If prepare runs out of time, it returns the rollouts that are still blocking and leaves admission closed. The controller then resumes, retires those rollouts and prepares again, so Gym never writes a checkpoint that is only partly consistent. If the controller itself crashes in the middle of a checkpoint, each participant's lease expires and it resumes on its own, so Gym never stays closed waiting for a controller that is gone.

    When a write fails or races with resume

    A commit repeated after its write failed stores the same state again and returns the same reply, since the state was taken only once. If resume arrives while a manifest is being written, it waits for the write's lock, and once resume returns no manifest can appear, so the controller's view and the files on disk never disagree.

    When work finishes or arrives at an awkward moment

    An episode that finishes during prepare stops at its final boundary with its result instead of replying, so the result cannot be lost between Gym's commit and the controller's own checkpoint. A replay step that ends while a checkpoint is open keeps its result until resume, leaving the saved boundary where it was. A model call that is still generating has its response held and its rows left out, and after a crash the agent makes it again, possibly continuing a cut prefix, which matches the saved state because the agent was saved before the call.

    When a rollout cannot be saved

    A rollout that touches a server unable to save it is listed as a restart, left out of the checkpoint and allowed to keep running while every other rollout is saved. If its session start reports this in the middle of a checkpoint, the episode is marked only after the checkpoint ends, and session starts on such servers wait for resume, so neither the saved state nor the restart list changes while the checkpoint is open.

    When an attempt is abandoned

    A request that arrives after its attempt was retired is refused with 409 stale_attempt until the controller forgets the rollout, so late requests can never mix rows into a later attempt. A retire that runs out of time leaves the episode tracked, blocking the next checkpoint until a repeated retire finishes it, so an episode that is only partly stopped is never saved.

    When a worker dies in the middle of a /run, the client sees a dropped connection. With checkpointing on, it does not send the /run again; the controller sees no reply and retires the attempt everywhere, which frees the sessions it started. Sending it again would have run the attempt twice and left the first run's sessions with nothing to free them.

    When a restore repeats or goes unused

    If the same checkpoint is restored twice and the continued rollout made model calls in between, the second restore deletes what those runs left, fences included, and starts from exactly the saved lineage. A restored rollout that is never sent again is deleted by the next commit that leaves it out, without a fence, so the controller can still start that attempt later. A new attempt that has already started is never deleted this way: its ledger is kept even if a commit leaves it out, so a running attempt's training rows are never lost.

    When workers come and go

    If a worker of a policy model server leaves, restore is refused until the server restarts, because its replacement cannot report what it served. If the number of workers changes between a checkpoint and its restore, sessions are installed on the live workers and every router receives the tables mapping old owners and sessions to their new workers, so old cookies keep reaching their sessions.

    Choices and the alternatives they rule out

    The mechanism as a whole is not small, because the problem spans several independent servers. Each part of it, though, is the simplest option we found that still meets the requirements. Where a cheaper option exists, the paragraphs below name it and explain which requirement it fails.

    Where state is saved

    Gym saves each rollout at the boundary after its last completed step rather than copying each server's memory. Copying the memory of several independent processes cannot produce one consistent moment unless every process stops at once, whereas boundaries are exactly where the protocol is already consistent.

    Servers declare what they can save in code rather than configuration, since only the author knows and a setting could claim support the code lacks. Every server takes part by default, and anything it cannot save restarts. If servers had to opt in instead, one that did not would be missing from every checkpoint without any error. Taking part by default costs some repeated work, never correctness.

    What happens to work in progress

    The policy model holds undelivered responses instead of waiting for generations to finish, which keeps prepare to seconds rather than minutes. The agent is still at its boundary before the call, so making the call again after a crash is exact. Generation cuts stay optional for the same reason: requiring every generation to continue would make every checkpoint depend on every inference worker, while a missing cut only means the call is generated again.

    Gym also does not hold finished results until the controller confirms receipt. A result the controller never received is simply a rollout still in flight in the controller's checkpoint, so it restarts, which is always correct, and dropping the acknowledgement removes a whole protocol along with the ways it could stall. Rollouts that cannot be saved are reported rather than waited for, because waiting stopped every checkpoint behind one such rollout and discarded its progress even when nothing crashed.

    How state reaches its end of life

    Retire stops the work and frees the state before it replies. Freeing in the background, or expiring state after a time, would depend on requests never arriving late, which Gym cannot promise. The refusal that outlives a retire ends with an explicit forget for the same reason: only the controller knows when a rollout is finished for good, and a time limit would delete the entry while a late request could still arrive. More generally, Gym has no time-based cleanup anywhere, because a cutoff can delete state a long rollout still uses and leaves everything else in place until it passes.

    A /run is never sent twice with checkpointing on. Sending it again after a dropped connection runs the attempt twice and strands the first run's sessions, whereas not sending it costs only one rerun of that rollout as its next attempt.

    How the order and the files stay consistent

    Gym decides the checkpoint order because it depends on which Gym server calls which. Keeping the order inside Gym lets the controller treat Gym as one system and makes it impossible to get the order wrong from outside.

    Each checkpoint is written once, to files that never change once named. Rewriting the state on every repeated commit could change a checkpoint after part of it was published, while naming the records file after its content and creating the manifest only once means a published checkpoint cannot change and racing writers cannot mix their files.

    Requests find their worker through a signed owner ID rather than a shared session table, which would add a lookup to every request and grow with every session served. The owner ID travels in the cookie or MCP token the client already sends.

    How long checkpoints take

    These runs used one workstation with every Gym server and a fake inference backend. Each rollout was a single_agent_turn weather episode with token capture and generation cuts on, and each rollout's second model call was held so that most rollouts were in flight at the checkpoint. Each run took a checkpoint, killed every Gym process, restarted Gym, restored, and ran the new attempts to completion.

    RolloutsPolicy workersIn flight and savedPrepare (s)Commit (s)Restore (s)New attempts that failed
    8,00014,2010.670.600.600
    8,00024,0830.560.690.560
    16,000214,3207.574.644.970
    16,0002, second run12,2283.601.833.230

    These numbers come from the branches this stack was cut from, and at 16,000 rollouts almost all of the prepare time is the policy model's.

    The slow paths that were fixed

    PathBeforeAfterChange
    Cleaning up 16,000 restored rollouts over 96,000 ledger filesabout 19 min0.23 sList the directory once and index it by rollout, instead of scanning it again for each rollout.
    Importing ledgers for 15,686 episodes3.2 s1.5 sSkip syncing each file to disk, since the checkpoint is the durable copy, and sync the directory once.

    Work the design repeats on purpose

    The design accepts some repeated work in order to stay correct, and none of it grows over the run. A rollout that cannot be saved starts over after a crash, though without a crash it costs nothing, and a held model call is generated again after a crash unless its prefix was cut. The policy model also does not know which rollouts are restarts, so it still holds their model calls during a checkpoint and may cut them for nothing. With several workers, commit and restore carry every worker's records through the coordinator's socket, with a 1 GiB limit per message, so a server with very large sessions would eventually need one records file per worker.

    How it is tested

    Example tests check what each operation does on its own. Most bugs found in review only appeared when operations overlapped or failed part way, so two kinds of tests cover that instead:

    • Contract tests over many inputs, wherever two pieces of code must agree: every payload the record check accepts is restored unchanged or fails the commit by name; every capture key built from a run request decodes back to the same rollout and attempt; every control route refuses an invalid request with a typed client error; every kind of corrupt manifest is a typed error.
    • Random sequences of operations against one participant in one process, and against a coordinator with several workers over its real socket. Each seed interleaves episode steps with prepare, commit, resume, retire, forget and restore at short or long deadlines, while writes are held or fail, cleanup is slow, a worker's close fails, workers join, and checkpoints restore onto a different number of workers. After every step: admission is open everywhere when idle; every worker refuses the same retired attempts as its coordinator; every manifest verifies and stores the checkpoint's first export; no manifest appears after resume; no commit includes a retired attempt or a running restart; and every committed checkpoint restores. Run against earlier versions of the stack, these fail on the bugs review found there.
    • Process-level tests start real Gym servers against a fake inference backend, checkpoint them mid-episode, kill them, restore, and check the exact model calls that follow, with one and with two workers per server. They include a deployment that mixes a saved environment with a restart-only one, and rollout collection preempted by a signal and resumed.
    • Every new test is checked against the code before its change, where it must fail.
    • An adversarial review pass before each push, reading the change for overlapping operations, partial failures, mismatched contracts, untyped errors and unbounded state.

    Known gaps

    Each gap below describes what Gym does today, what goes wrong, and the change that would fix it. Where Gym falls back to restarting a rollout or failing a checkpoint, the result is slower but still correct. The four gaps tagged fixed could produce a wrong or failed rollout, or leave state behind, and are fixed in the stack; they stay here so reviewers can see what changed.

    A new model call during a checkpoint waits instead of failing fixed

    The policy model used to answer a new call during a checkpoint with 409 admission_closed. Simple Agent coped by returning to its boundary, but a restart keeps running through the checkpoint, and an agent without hooks would have shown the error to the model or failed the rollout. A new call now waits until resume before it is admitted, as a resources server's requests already did. Because a waiting call is never admitted, prepare does not count it, and if its attempt is retired while it waits, it is refused at once with stale_attempt instead of running after resume. The proof refinement agent's retry loop for the old refusal is gone, since nothing sends that refusal any more.

    A rollout sent after the last checkpoint is never sent again as the same attempt fixed

    After a crash, the evaluation controller used to send every unfinished rollout outside the checkpoint again with the same attempt number, and nothing retired the earlier run's copy. A harness from that run could still be alive in a remote sandbox, and its calls would have been accepted into the new run. Rollout collection now keeps a dispatch log, described under evaluation runs, and on resume it retires the last attempt the previous run sent of every unfinished rollout it does not restore, then sends the next one. Only rows that were actually sent are retired, so resuming a large evaluation retires only the rows its previous run sent and did not finish, not every row it has left. The attempt number is excluded from every metric, so the bump changes capture keys but not results.

    Saving an opaque harness through sandbox snapshots needs two more pieces open

    An agent can already save a harness running in a microVM-backed sandbox through its session hooks, but two things are missing before that works end to end. First, nothing tells a server when a checkpoint is deleted, so the snapshots its saved state names would never be freed; the controller needs to pass the IDs of the checkpoints it keeps so servers can free the rest. Second, the harness is usually waiting on a model or tool call at the moment its sandbox is paused, and after a crash that call's connection points at a server that no longer exists and carries the old attempt. The restored harness must have that call reach the restored model under the next attempt, either through the harness's own retry or through something in front of it that resends the call.

    A session start sent twice can leave a copy on another worker open

    If a session start's reply is lost while both servers keep running, the caller sends it again, and with several workers on the receiving server the second request can land on a different worker. The first copy then stays on its worker with nothing to free it until the server restarts. Not resending a session start once it may have been received, or routing session starts by session ID, would close this.

    A crash right after a group's comparison delays its members slow

    Members that had not recorded their reward wait 30 minutes, fail and restart from their input. Recording the group's result before replying to any member would remove the wait.

    The evaluation controller repeats a retire that fails fixed

    Rollout collection used to log a failed batch of retires and move on, so the servers that missed it kept the attempts' state for the rest of the run. It now keeps every attempt whose retire failed and repeats them before the next checkpoint and again when the run ends. A forget that fails was already safe, because the run forgets every rollout it retired when it ends.

    Files left by a killed process are removed by the next server fixed

    A server with several workers used to put its coordinator socket at $TMPDIR/ng-<kind>-<pid>-<random>.sock and never remove it, and session routing removed its directory of worker sockets only on a clean exit, so every crash left files behind. Each server process now has one runtime directory, /tmp/ng-<pid>-<random>/, that holds its coordinator socket and its workers' private sockets and is removed when the process exits. Creating one first removes those that killed servers left behind, and a directory counts as left behind only if its owning process no longer exists and none of its sockets accepts a connection. The second check protects a live server in another container that shares /tmp but not the process namespace, and since neither check is about age, a live server's directory is never removed. A connection that times out counts as alive, so a busy server is never mistaken for a dead one.

    A write killed in the middle can also leave .records.jsonl.<random> or .manifest.json.<random> inside a participant's part of a checkpoint. These need no change: nothing reads them, because the manifest names the real file, and they go when the controller deletes that checkpoint.

    A /run the controller itself sends twice open

    A second /run for an attempt that is already running can end the live episode. Making /run idempotent is planned as separate work.

    A restored cut can be lost with several workers compute only

    A worker takes a restored cut when it claims it, so if the claim times out the call is generated again, which costs compute but is still correct.

    This stack has not yet been run against a real model, a real inference worker serving generation cuts, or a deployment across several hosts. The process-level tests use a fake inference backend.

    What any controller must do

    Gym's guarantees hold only if the controller does its part, and each rule below covers something Gym cannot enforce on its own.

    • Pause between prepare and resume. Stop sending rollouts and stop anything that consumes them, and do not read capture manifests or call the capture retire and delete routes while Gym is prepared or committed.
    • Leave restarts out of the commit. Build the commit list with PrepareResult.continued, and keep naming each continued rollout in every commit until its next attempt has been sent.
    • Wait for replies already on the way. Before building the checkpoint's list of rollouts, wait for every /run reply whose rollout is not in the commit.
    • Publish before resuming. Publish the checkpoint only after every commit has succeeded, then call resume.
    • Record what you send, and retire it before sending again. Record each attempt somewhere that outlives your process before you send it, including the rollouts sent after your last checkpoint. After a crash, retire the last recorded attempt of every rollout that will start over, then send it from its input as the next attempt, and send continued rollouts as their next attempt. Restore a checkpoint only if no later run of yours sent its rollouts again.
    • Resume before retiring a straggler. To give up on a rollout that blocks prepare, resume first, retire it, then prepare again.
    • Forget when finished. Call forget once a retired rollout can never run again.
    • Repeat a call that fails until it succeeds. No call is atomic across servers, so a retire or forget that fails partway must be repeated, or the servers that missed it keep the attempt's state or its entry.
    • Delete checkpoint directories you do not keep. That includes directories from commits that were never published, which may hold partial records or temporary files from a crashed write.
    • Keep each group's group attempt. Changing it on restore would leave grouped verification waiting forever.

    Control API

    Every participating server exposes the same bearer-protected routes. Gym's checkpoint coordination calls them in the required order; the training framework calls the coordination.

    RouteValid in phaseEffect
    POST /ng-control/v1/checkpoint/prepareidle, preparingclose admission, then wait until ready or the deadline; report blockers, and the restarts that never block
    POST …/retireidle, restoredmark the named attempts' rollouts, stop their work, wait for it, free their state, then reply; refused while a checkpoint is open
    POST …/forgetidle, restoredstop refusing these rollouts' retired attempts, once the controller is done with them for good
    POST …/commitpreparedre-check readiness, export once, write records then manifest; a retry awaits the same write, or stores the same export again if storing failed; idempotent; a scope that names a restart is refused with 409 restart_in_scope
    POST …/restoreidle, fresh processread and validate the records in scope in one streaming pass, install them under the next attempt, stay closed; a retire waits for an install that outlived its deadline
    POST …/resumeany non-idlestop an unfinished write, so no manifest appears after it returns; reopen admission and let parked work continue; also the abort path
    GET …/statusanyphase, checkpoint ID, readiness report, and checkpoint mode; a resources server also reports whether its verification may be replayed
    POST /ng-control/v1/generation-cut (inference worker)—stage the prefix of each in-flight call and return a receipt

    Coordination order: prepare environment servers → policy model → agents → resources. Commit in any order. Every commit is scoped to the episodes the controller continues: those in flight except the restarts, which PrepareResult.continued leaves out, and each unclaimed restored episode under its replacement attempt. Resume resources → policy model → agents → environment servers. Retire callers before callees: environment servers → agents → policy model and resources together, each replying only after the attempts' work has stopped. After a commit writes its files, each participant also deletes the restored episodes that are neither running nor in the commit's scope. It does not retire them: the controller may still start those rollouts over as the same attempt, so nothing may refuse that attempt later, such as a capture-ledger fence. A replacement attempt that has started is never deleted this way. A restore gives each participant every episode it continues, including ones the participant holds no record of, so a participant that keeps files per episode clears what a dead execution left. A restore that misses its deadline reopens admission only once its install has finished. Restore is all or nothing: if any participant fails, coordination retires the replacement attempts everywhere, which frees their restored state, and resumes every participant. The training framework restarts those rollouts from their input as later attempts.

    Before its own barrier, the training framework waits for the replies to its outstanding /run calls whose episodes no participant exported. Those episodes finished before prepare was ready, so their replies are already in flight. This replaces a completed-result acknowledgement protocol: Gym never holds a finished result waiting for an acknowledgement, and a lost reply can never block a checkpoint.

    NeMo RL as the controller

    In training, NeMo RL's Gym actor is the controller. It calls the coordination functions directly and never addresses an individual Gym server, so the participant order lives entirely in Gym. Its own sequencing code for Gym's servers can be deleted.

    Pausing training around a checkpoint

    Between prepare and resume, NeMo RL pauses rollout dispatch, the trainer actors and the trajectory assembler actors, because any of them consuming or retiring rollouts during that window could break the cut Gym is writing. NeMo RL then saves its own checkpoint after Gym's commit has succeeded, records which rollouts continue and which restart, and only then resumes Gym. Rollouts whose replies were already on the wire must be collected before NeMo RL builds that list.

    Token data across the checkpoint

    The policy model's commit reply lists the staged token-store keys the checkpoint still refers to, both as one list and per rollout. NeMo RL keeps the rows of the rollouts it continues, and rows belonging to calls the checkpoint left out become orphans that are masked from training. With generation cuts on, NeMo RL's inference workers stage each cut prefix through the worker helpers in #3884, and the restored call continues it after the crash.

    NeMo RL also owns capture cleanup: it retires a rollout's capture once the result has been consumed or abandoned, and deletes it once nothing can still write to it. Those routes refuse with 409 during a checkpoint, so NeMo RL retries them after resume.

    After a crash

    After a restore, NeMo RL sends each continued rollout again as its next attempt and Gym continues it from its boundary. For each restart, and for every unfinished rollout that was not in the checkpoint, it first retires the last attempt and then sends the next attempt from its input. Groups for GenRM keep their group attempt, so the group re-forms once every member has verified again.

    Ending refusals

    NeMo RL must call forget once a retired rollout is finished for good, or every Gym server keeps one entry per retired rollout for the rest of the run. This requirement is new to NeMo RL's side and is tracked on NVIDIA-NeMo/RL#4549.

    Evaluation runs as the controller

    In evaluation runs, Gym's rollout collection is the controller, since it is the process that sends the rows. With checkpoint_dir set, it checkpoints on SIGUSR1 and keeps running, checkpoints on SIGTERM and stops, which lets a scheduler such as Slurm checkpoint just before a preemption, and can also checkpoint on a timer with checkpoint_every_s.

    Each checkpoint stops starting new rows, prepares, commits the rows whose /run has not replied except the restarts, writes the run's manifest with both lists, and publishes it by pointing LATEST at it. Only the two most recent checkpoints are kept. Rows whose /run got no reply are retired everywhere in batches between checkpoints, and a batch that fails is repeated before the next checkpoint and when the run ends.

    Every run also keeps a dispatch log in the checkpoint directory. It starts with the run's ID and gets one line for each attempt the run sends, written just before the /run that sends it, plus the attempts a restore installs and the fences a crashed run left behind. The log is flushed to the kernel but never synced: a killed process leaves its lines behind, and a crashed host takes its Gym servers down with it, so there is nothing left on it to fence.

    A run restarted with resume_from_cache=true reads that log and the latest checkpoint before sending anything. If the run that wrote the log also published the checkpoint, the checkpoint's rows are restored and continue as their next attempt. Every other unfinished row in the log, whether a restart or a row sent after the checkpoint, has its logged attempt retired everywhere and starts again from its input one attempt later. When the IDs differ, a later run crashed before its own first checkpoint and may have sent the checkpoint's rows again, so none of them is restored and they all start over, which is slower but never installs an attempt next to one still running. The new run forgets every rollout it retired once it ends.

    How the work is split into pull requests

    Every pull request is a single commit built from a branch head that passed its tests. The capture performance work is now its own set of pull requests against main: #4268 bounds the capture ledger's cache, #3937 replaces deleted lock files with striped ones, and #3938 and #3939 add retire and delete to the capture ledger and the record store. The checkpoint stack sits on #3939 because the policy model participant retires and deletes capture ledgers through those two; it does not need #4268 or #3937.
