    Part 3

    v1, as proposed

    This is the first proposal (17 September 2026), preserved unchanged for the record. It planned an episode processor that later landed on main as the environment server, and its implementation was the Gym pull-request chain #2939–#2946. Part 4 explains how v2 maps to it.
    Architecture decision · 17 September 2026

    Partial-rollout checkpointing for NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym

    owner ansubramania · aligned with episode orchestration PRs #3482–#3492 · checkpoint ownership update · self-contained HTML, inline CSS/JS/SVG

    The episode-orchestration design moves the complete rollout lifecycle out of an agent server's /run method and into an episode processor. The processor owns resources and agent session setup, one or more /v1/responses activations, verification, cleanup, and the decision about what happens next. Checkpointing must therefore persist the episode boundary in the processor. Agent servers persist only the private session state needed to continue later /v1/responses activations. NeMo-RL still owns the global checkpoint transaction and validates the processor, agent-session, resources, model-lineage, and TransferQueue records as one compatible cut.

    Requirements for a recoverable checkpoint

    These requirements define when a checkpoint is safe to publish and restore. The walkthrough shows where each requirement affects normal execution, checkpoint preparation, saving, and recovery.

    System constraints

    • Gym must commit before the global checkpoint is published. A slow rollout therefore cannot block checkpointing indefinitely.
    • Durable token state remains a training-framework responsibility. The Gym draft stores lineage and staging coordinates, not token, mask, or log-probability arrays. A production checkpoint may be published only after the controller has made the referenced TransferQueue rows durable and has verified the join. That controller and actual queue durability are not part of PRs #2939–#2946.
    • Recovery starts from the latest published checkpoint. Gym keeps server state in memory and serializes it only during a checkpoint commit. After an unplanned crash, NeMo-RL re-dispatches any later in-flight work from its input.
    • One leased SingleController dispatches rollouts and coordinates checkpoints. A second controller cannot run concurrently.
    • The design must support large live execution sets. Shared-filesystem metadata operations cannot grow linearly with the number of rollouts.

    Identity

    A rollout keeps one identity across attempts.

    NeMo-RL assigns rollout_id before dispatch and preserves it across retries and restores. Each fresh dispatch or restore increments _ng_attempt_index. The attempt-qualified path (…-aN) identifies captured transport data, not the logical rollout. Every artifact, control call, and result carries the rollout ID and attempt index as separate fields.

    Servers reject stale attempts.

    A model, resources, or runtime mutation receives HTTP 409 when it carries an obsolete attempt index. Restore may add tombstones for abandoned call roots, but it cannot remove or reassign them. Final attribution ignores every tombstoned root.

    Admission and quiescence

    Closing a gate and testing admission happen atomically.

    The AdmissionLimiter grants a capacity permit only while the gate accepts work. Closing the gate atomically rejects or parks new callers. A caller waiting for capacity holds no permit and does not count as in flight. An admitted request remains in flight until its response and required custody updates are durable.

    Only policy model servers pause in the first milestone.

    Token-capture checkpointing first closes admission only on policy model-server instances backed by NeMo-RL generation workers. Stateless resources servers and verifiers retain no checkpoint state and do not need an admission API. Stateful-resources support later closes admission on those resources-server instances as well. Judge and simulator model-server instances remain open so accepted tools and verifiers can finish. Startup validation rejects environment traffic that targets a policy instance.

    A model-server pause must cover every FastAPI worker process.

    A pause request routed to one Uvicorn worker cannot close admission for the other workers that share the service port. The PR stack implements and tests a service-level coordinator protocol over a Unix-domain socket. Workers apply coordinator state and report acknowledgements plus local in-flight counts. The coordinator reports paused only after every expected worker has acknowledged the checkpoint ID and the summed count is zero. Production startup and control-URL routing are not wired yet, so a configured multi-worker server reports unmanaged and NeMo-RL must refuse checkpointing through it. Single-worker servers are the supported first integration.

    Prepare parks episode processors before it closes their dependencies.

    POST /ng-control/v1/episode-checkpoint/prepare changes active episodes to park_requested. Each processor finishes its current protocol operation, records an EpisodeBoundaryRecord, and blocks on an in-memory event. The boundary identifies the next protocol operation and every still-open agent and resources session. NeMo-RL prepares those component sessions and closes policy-model admission only after the processor has stopped issuing new calls. Judge and simulator model instances remain open while an accepted operation finishes.

    Resources mutations finish before state export.

    The resources middleware serializes mutations for each rollout attempt with an asyncio.Lock. Resources prepare closes admission, acquires each live session's lock, and exports that session after any accepted mutation releases the lock. New mutations receive 409 admission_closed. The first integration does not propagate admission leases or expose separate resources-admission routes.

    The controller decides what happens to unfinished rollouts.

    The Gym routes expose blockers and provide attempt-specific model abort, agent retirement, and resources retirement. Resources retirement is checkpoint-fenced and waits for that execution's mutation lock before it removes adapter state and the prepared snapshot. A future controller must decide whether all participant state for a straggler can be discarded. If an external effect cannot be rolled back or acknowledged, the controller must abort the global checkpoint rather than publish an incomplete cut.

    Ordering

    Generation workers stay available during prepare.

    Accepted generations must finish staging their output before Gym can drain. Pausing workers earlier would deadlock prepare. NeMo-RL may pause, checkpoint, or refit workers only after Gym commits and before the final resume.

    The future controller must finish finalizers before saving TransferQueue.

    Pausing Gym does not stop an RL-side finalizer that is already writing token rows. The training-framework integration must wait for those writes, publish a completed group before clearing staged rows, and then save the queue. This ordering is not implemented by the Gym stack.

    Each manifest is written last.

    A component writes payloads to temporary names, flushes them, and renames them before writing its manifest. The actor verifies every component digest before writing gym/manifest.json. The SingleController writes training_info.json last, renames the checkpoint atomically, and flushes the parent directory. A committed participant directory never changes.

    One explicit call resumes work in dependency order.

    Prepare, commit, and restore leave Gym paused. After the checkpoint is published and generation workers pass validation, NemoGym.resume opens resources admission and policy model admission, reconnects agent sessions and runtimes, releases parked episode processors, and finally reopens dispatch. A processor cannot resume before every session referenced by its boundary is usable.

    Durability and publication

    TransferQueue needs its own durable snapshot contract.

    The intended training checkpoint uses a fresh content-addressed path and restores it by the digest recorded in the global checkpoint. The Gym stack neither defines nor exercises that persistence operation; it only stores the coordinates that the controller must validate against the restored queue.

    Gym components publish immutable manifests after their payloads.

    The current draft writes one JSON payload per parked boundary or resources snapshot and copies token-free lineage files, then writes a digest-bearing manifest last. The episode-oriented design adds separate processor-boundary and private agent-session manifests. This makes torn writes and corrupt restore input detectable. Archive shards with a member index can replace per-rollout files later without changing the checkpoint APIs or state machine.

    Control operations are idempotent and fenced.

    Every actor method and control endpoint carries checkpoint_id and an absolute deadline. Repeating a phase for the same checkpoint returns the recorded result. A stale checkpoint ID cannot reopen traffic or replace files. A mutex in the NemoGym actor serializes checkpoint phase changes and live-execution snapshots. It prevents two checkpoint IDs from preparing concurrently, prevents commit, abort, restore, and resume from racing, and rejects invalid transitions such as commit before prepared. Participant I/O is deadline-bounded, and the lock-free checkpoint_status snapshot keeps progress observable while an operation is active.

    Restore

    NeMo-RL chooses one recovery action for each execution.

    An execution is already complete, resumes from an episode boundary, resumes from a full runtime snapshot, or starts again from its input. An execution marked transferred_to_rl cannot also have a continuation. The restored NeMo-RL registry decides whether work completed or failed. Gym does not make that decision.

    Gym restores participants paused; the controller verifies the full join.

    Each participant restores attempt-N state as attempt N+1 and remains closed until an explicit resume. The model participant rejects a non-fresh ledger namespace. The resources participant requires a fresh process that has not served stateful traffic. Agent servers restore only the sessions named by selected episode boundaries. Episode processors restore last, after the controller verifies their last model-call IDs, resources revisions, agent-session snapshots, and restored TransferQueue rows.

    An opaque harness requires a full runtime snapshot.

    A filesystem snapshot, sandbox identifier, or provider descriptor cannot restore an opaque harness by itself. A resumable snapshot includes the harness process tree and memory, the egress relay's pending requests and cached responses, and a provider compatibility fingerprint. At the prepare deadline, the runtime may freeze a forwarded but unfinished request as pending reissue. Restore tombstones the abandoned server-side call and sends a new request through the relay.

    The processor owns protocol state; servers own private session state

    The ownership rule is: the component that decides the next remote operation persists the state needed to make that decision. The episode processor decides whether to seed a session, invoke /v1/responses, verify, close, or return. It therefore owns the episode boundary. An agent server owns only state hidden behind agent_session_id that is needed to service a later activation. Resources and model servers continue to own environment state and model-call lineage.

    Do not persist the same mutable fact in two ownersThe processor may retain the request and response exchanged with an agent. The agent may retain an internal conversation or native thread cursor when that state is not supplied on the wire. It must be clear which copy is authoritative. A processor-supplied full conversation and an independently mutable agent-side conversation cannot both determine the next turn.

    State the agent server persists

    StateWhy it belongs to the agent serverCheckpoint rule
    Session identityagent_session_id, EpisodeId, and TaskId bind later /v1/responses and close calls to the same private session.Restore under attempt N+1 with a new externally visible session identity or a validated attempt remapping. Attempt N remains fenced.
    Private agent continuationNative thread IDs, compaction summaries, graph cursors, harness state, or other data that the processor cannot reconstruct from the Responses request and response.Export a versioned typed snapshot only at a declared activation boundary. If the state cannot be serialized, advertise restart_only or require a full runtime snapshot.
    Scoped dependency accessThe resources transport, resources cookies, sandbox connection descriptor, and work directory supplied when the session is seeded are inputs to the agent implementation.Persist serializable descriptors and cookie values, never live clients, sockets, subprocess objects, or callback functions. Validate the restored descriptors before accepting an activation.
    Accumulated agent observationsModel, tool, compaction, child-invocation, and conversation observations returned by the agent close response may be assembled inside the agent runtime.Retain observations not yet transferred to the processor. Release them only after close or an explicit durable acknowledgement.
    Activation deduplicationA retry after a lost response must not execute the same logical activation twice when the agent has private mutable state or external effects.Record the logical activation ID, request digest, completion status, and response digest for the latest replayable activation.

    The agent server does not own the materialized task, the episode's next protocol stage, verification status, resources state, model token rows, or global recovery disposition. A stateless agent whose complete input arrives in each /v1/responses request may have no checkpoint payload beyond admission, attempt fencing, and any unacknowledged close observations.

    State the episode processor persists

    StateRequired contentCheckpoint rule
    Identity and protocolEpisodeId, TaskId, processor type and schema version, materialized task input or its immutable reference.The restored processor must prove that it is continuing the same task and protocol under attempt N+1.
    Next operationA typed stage such as seed_resources, seed_agent, invoke_agent, close_agent, verify, close_resources, or return_result, plus an invocation index.Commit only after the preceding operation has a durable outcome. Never serialize a coroutine or infer the stage from which handles happen to exist.
    Open participant handlesresources_session_id, agent_session_id, cookie values, tool-access metadata, sandbox descriptors, and the participant instance names that own them.Every referenced participant snapshot must appear in the same aggregate checkpoint. Cleanup ownership is persisted as data: open, close pending, or closed.
    Completed operation resultsThe latest complete agent response or durable reference, agent-close observations, verification input, verification result when complete, and any partial result required by the protocol.Retain a result until the next operation has durably consumed it. Use request and response digests to make retries idempotent.
    Cross-component joinsLast committed policy model-call ID, expected resources revision, agent activation ID, and any runtime or token-custody reference needed by recovery.NeMo-RL validates these joins against model, resources, agent-session, runtime, and TransferQueue manifests before releasing the processor.
    Outcome and cleanup obligationsHandled failure, retryability, terminal status, and which sessions or runtimes still require close, detach, or destroy.EpisodeContext callbacks are process-local conveniences. The durable boundary must contain enough data to retry cleanup after process loss.

    State that must not be checkpointed as application data

    Neither owner serializes active HTTP requests, asyncio tasks, semaphores, locks, clients, sockets, file descriptors, or arbitrary process memory. Prepare either waits for the current operation to reach a durable boundary, retires a restart-safe attempt, or delegates an opaque runtime to a provider that can snapshot and restore the complete process plus its egress state.

    Logical rollout and attempt identity

    rollout_id identifies the logical work across failures. attempt_index identifies one execution of that work. Restore never reactivates attempt N. It installs state for attempt N+1 and tombstones attempt N, so delayed HTTP requests from the old process receive 409 stale_attempt instead of mutating restored state.

    Episode processor execution state

    A boundary is the completed state after a whole protocol operation, not a separate execution state. While the processor is invoking the agent for activation 5, its boundary after activation 4 may remain available as a rollback point, but it is publishable only if every component still agrees with that earlier point. Prepare changes running to park_requested. The processor finishes the current operation, commits the next boundary, and then blocks on an in-memory event.

    The processor participant reports whether each parked episode has a committed boundary. Both a park without a boundary and a completed result that NeMo-RL has not durably acknowledged make ready_to_commit false. Agent-session and resources participants report their own matching state; the processor boundary does not substitute for those snapshots.

    If the deadline expires between boundaries, prepare fails without inventing a successful result. Retirement cancels the processor's outer /run task and any active component request, retires the referenced agent and resources sessions, and tombstones the attempt. Retirement is not durable result acknowledgement: a completed-but-unacknowledged episode continues to block publication.

    Checkpoint phase and admission state

    The control fence is per server process and per checkpoint ID. It prevents a stale or concurrent controller from committing, restoring, or resuming the wrong transaction. Repeating the same successful operation returns its recorded result. Most failed operations return to their entry phase. Model restore is deliberately different: a failure leaves both the limiter and the control fence in restore_failed_paused, so status remains observable and the same restore can be retried or explicitly resumed without admitting traffic by accident.

    Admission is a separate state machine. The policy model server changes from accepting to draining when prepare closes its gate. A request is prepare-safe only after durable completed custody, a durable failure, a validated active-prefix receipt, a no-generation exit, or complete pre-cut response egress. Response lifetime remains separate: a response that has not started is fenced until checkpoint resolution, while a stream that already started drains completely instead of entering a prefix cut. Missing workers, duplicate worker IDs, swallowed cancellation, and incomplete receipts fail closed. New requests receive 409 admission_closed. Resume reopens admission and releases fenced response egress after commit or restore.

    What the current Gym draft guarantees

    The model, agent-session, resources, and episode-processor participants preserve separate parts of one attempt-N cut and install them for attempt N+1 while traffic remains paused. Their manifests are separated by participant instance inside one controller-supplied directory. Active generation receipts bind immutable worker, model-call, frozen-buffer, inventory, and backend-snapshot identities. The production guarantee depends on a controller that checks every manifest and the matching TransferQueue snapshot before publishing one global checkpoint.

    The Python implementation is intentionally internal

    The checkpoint modules in PRs #2940–#2946 live under nemo_gym._checkpoint. The leading underscore marks this as an experimental implementation rather than a supported public import surface. Gym servers use these modules internally while the protocol, controller integration, and storage format continue to evolve. A later stabilization change can expose a public package after those contracts are ready for compatibility guarantees.

    Work remaining outside the Gym draft stack

    • Integrate the NemoGym actor participant from NeMo-RL #4093 into the existing SingleController checkpoint transaction, including global publication, restored rollout disposition, and training-state reconciliation.
    • Reuse NeMo-RL's existing native TransferQueue save and restore from #3429 and #3480. Add Gym-manifest reconciliation against that restored inventory and implement production inference-generation cuts.
    • Wire the multi-worker coordinator into Gym process startup and route one authenticated control URL per server instance. Until then, require num_workers=1.
    • Apply deadline_ts inside commit, restore, and resume operations. Those request models carry the deadline today, but only prepare and model-drain waits actively enforce it.
    • Pack per-rollout payloads into bounded archive shards before using the format at very large rollout counts.

    How the components share checkpoint ownership

    The existing NeMo-RL SingleController owns the global checkpoint transaction, including a data-plane checkpoint barrier, native TransferQueue save and restore, rollout-recovery state, replay metadata, and atomic publication. The episode processor owns each externally dispatched /run lifecycle and the protocol boundary between resources seed, agent seed, /v1/responses activation, agent close, verification, resources close, and result return. Agent servers own private state behind agent_session_id. The policy model server owns admission and token-free lineage. Stateful resources servers own environment sessions, revisions, and exact-once mutation receipts. NeMo-RL #4093 must be updated to discover episode processors, order all participant routes, freeze actor-local membership, validate aggregate manifests, and acknowledge completed episode results.

    The processor boundary replaces the agent /run boundary

    The existing checkpoint draft places conversation, control phase, cookies, model-call identity, and resources revisions in AgentBoundaryRecord. Under episode orchestration, that record splits. EpisodeBoundaryRecord retains protocol position, request and response data, participant handles, cleanup obligations, and cross-component joins. AgentSessionSnapshot retains only private agent implementation state that cannot be reconstructed from the processor's request and response history.

    Normal rollout execution records restorable state

    Each component records the state it already owns during normal execution. The actor registers episodes. The episode processor records the latest completed protocol operation and the handles it still owns. Agent servers retain private session state across /v1/responses activations. The model server records token custody, generation workers stage tokens, and resources servers retain sessions. Checkpointing adds in-memory boundaries and receipts but no per-rollout filesystem writes during this phase.

    Prepare stops new work and reaches a recoverable boundary

    The intended NeMo-RL flow first stops new episode dispatch and asks each episode processor to prepare. Active processors finish their current protocol operation and park after committing a boundary. NeMo-RL then prepares every agent and resources session named by those boundaries and pauses policy-model admission. If a processor misses the deadline, references an uncheckpointable session, or reports an unsafe parked or completed state, prepare fails. A controller may retire a restart-safe attempt and retry, but Gym does not silently discard it.

    Save publishes only a complete checkpoint

    Gym accepts one controller-owned directory and writes frozen model, agent-session, resources, and episode-processor state into separate namespaces beneath it. Each component publishes a digest-bearing manifest last and remains paused until explicit resume. The controller must stop its rollout registry and TransferQueue writers, invoke those commits, save the queue, validate every artifact, and publish the global checkpoint. The current checkpoint draft implements the first three server participants under the older agent-owned /run boundary; episode orchestration requires the processor and agent-session split described here.

    Restore verifies each continuation before dispatch

    Replacement Gym processes restore model lineage, resources sessions, and agent sessions while admission remains closed. Episode processor boundaries restore only after those dependencies exist. The resources process must be fresh, and every participant requires a separate explicit resume. The controller verifies each processor boundary against the matching agent session, resources revision, model-call lineage, and restored token inventory. The first resumed policy call carries the verified attempt-N source capture key and parent model-call ID exactly once.

    The current test proves the pre-processor participant mechanics

    The top PR, Gym #2946, contains tests/unit_tests/test_checkpoint_e2e.py. The test proves fencing, model lineage, agent-owned boundaries, resources snapshots, retirement, restore, and one-shot parent relay. It predates the episode processor ownership split. It remains useful participant-level evidence, but it is not the target end-to-end episode recovery test.

    The replacement test needs a fourth manifestThe episode-oriented test must park and commit an episode processor boundary, restore its referenced model, resources, and agent-session state first, then restore the processor and verify that it continues with the next protocol operation. The test must also prove that process-local cleanup callbacks can be lost without losing durable cleanup obligations.

    Behavior exercised by the test

    1. Agent prepare rejects a parked execution with no committed boundary and a completed result with no durable training-framework acknowledgement.
    2. A restart-safe straggler is retired from the agent and resources participants and aborted in model admission. Its model lineage is excluded from the committed cut.
    3. The model, agent, and resources participants write three separate manifests beneath the same controller directory. The model manifest is namespaced by server name; the agent manifest is namespaced by a stable hash of the configured instance name; the resources manifest is namespaced by server name.
    4. Fresh replacement processes restore the surviving rollout as attempt N+1 and reject model, agent, and resources traffic before explicit resume.
    5. After resume, the resources revision and state are available under N+1. The first policy call receives the attempt-N source capture key and parent call. Its copied lineage retains the parent's staging key, weight version, lengths, digests, mode, staging chain, chain hash, and cumulative hash.
    6. The relay headers are consumed once. The next policy call carries no attempt-N parent headers and resolves to the first call recorded within N+1.

    Boundary of this end-to-end test

    The Gym test simulates controller ordering with direct route calls. Separate tests in NeMo-RL #4093 exercise the NemoGym actor against the pinned Gym stack. NeMo-RL separately tests its existing SingleController and native TransferQueue recovery. The missing joined test inserts the actor and Gym manifests into that real controller transaction and validates their model coordinates against the restored token inventory.

    Why component-owned boundaries are the default

    The central constraint is not writing bytes to disk. It is choosing a point where the agent conversation, resources state, model-call lineage, and token rows describe the same completed work. The Gym draft APIs let each server finish the operation it owns and freeze its local state. The remaining NeMo-RL integration must coordinate those participants and verify the cross-component join without importing each environment's private representation.

    Normal execution pays memory and synchronization costs, not checkpoint I/O

    PathAdditional work during normal executionExpected effect
    Every internal requestRead two request-scoped values and attach x-ng-rollout-id plus x-ng-attempt-index. Validate that explicit headers do not conflict with the active context.Small fixed CPU and header overhead. No filesystem operation and no extra network round trip.
    Episode processor /runInsert one execution object into an in-memory dictionary. After each complete protocol operation, validate and replace one EpisodeBoundaryRecord containing the next operation, open session handles, completed inputs and outputs, cleanup obligations, model-call ID, and resource revision.Memory grows with live episodes and retained protocol state. Boundary construction adds serialization and copying at operation boundaries but no normal-path fsync.
    Agent /v1/responsesFor a stateful session, update private continuation state and retain one replayable activation receipt. A stateless agent performs no additional checkpoint bookkeeping.Cost depends on the agent. The checkpoint contract must not force every Responses API agent to retain a duplicate conversation when the processor already supplies complete input.
    Policy model requestParse identity headers, check admission and tombstones, create one in-memory ticket, and remove it after the ASGI response completes. Capture-enabled requests already perform the more expensive token-staging and lineage work required by the token-capture stack.Small fixed bookkeeping cost per generation. The limiter does not add a queue or remote coordinator call on the single-worker data path.
    Stateful resources mutationParse identity and request ID, acquire an asyncio.Lock for that rollout attempt, buffer and validate the complete response, then atomically advance the revision and retain a replayable receipt before egress. Successful terminal operations unregister the session while preserving bounded receipt evidence.This is the largest semantic cost. Mutations for one session become serialized and their responses are buffered. Different sessions still run concurrently. Environments that already require ordered state changes should not lose useful parallelism.
    Server startupInstall the capabilities route and checkpoint participants. A multi-worker deployment reports unmanaged until the production coordinator lifecycle is wired.No per-request cost beyond the middleware described above. Capability negotiation occurs only during startup and restore.

    Checkpoint-time cost is proportional to live state. Prepare waits for accepted processor operations and component activations, copies episode, agent-session, and resources state into frozen sets, and commits those sets to disk. Large live sets may create excessive shared-filesystem metadata traffic. Archive shards and a member index remain a later storage optimization.

    Cleanup obligations survive processor failure

    EpisodeContext may still use LIFO callbacks during normal execution, but the durable episode boundary records which agent sessions, resources sessions, and runtimes remain open. A replacement processor can therefore finish cleanup after the original process dies. Tombstones remain separate so delayed attempt-N traffic is rejected. Completed episode results remain cached until the receipt-bound acknowledgement validates identity and result digest. NeMo-RL #4093 performs that acknowledgement only after the result crosses the actor boundary.

    A generation-safe cut separates request lifetime from durable token custody

    The restacked Gym drafts implement the active-generation inventory, cut, durable receipt, worker-membership aggregation, response-egress fence, and restore validation contracts described here. Deterministic fake-backend tests cover close-before-egress, started-stream drain, cancellation, worker replacement, receipt mismatch, and multi-worker omission. #3218 and its inference children track the remaining real vLLM and Megatron cuts plus reconciliation with NeMo-RL's existing checkpointed TransferQueue.

    Part of the cutMeaning at checkpoint timeRequired invariant
    Response lifetimeThe HTTP or engine request remains active until its response is published, cancelled, or fenced. Request liveness is not itself durable token custody.The checkpoint records whether the response existed at the cut and prevents the old attempt from publishing after replacement.
    Completed durable custodyToken segments completed before the cut are already owned by the framework token store and included in the selected durable snapshot.Gym lineage names the same immutable segments that the framework validates before global publication.
    Active pre-cut prefixFor an accepted generation still decoding, the engine atomically detaches the tokens produced before the cut from tokens produced afterward. The detached prefix is staged durably before the checkpoint can publish.The cut has one acknowledged token boundary. Post-cut decoding cannot alter or republish the pre-cut segment.
    Prefix delivery after restoreThe restored child generation receives the durable pre-cut prefix through the representation supported by its engine.Delivery changes representation, not custody, identity, length, or hash.

    #3227 proposes staged-prefix cuts for NeMo-RL vLLM generation. A worker with access to TransferQueue receives a staging chain and fetches the prefix itself. #3228 proposes inline-prefix recovery for Megatron Inference. In that path, NeMo-RL materializes the same durable staging chain and sends the token IDs inline. The staged and inline forms are mutually exclusive delivery mechanisms for one custody record.

    Prefix custody is common, but prefix delivery differs by inference backend

    Hashes and lineage keys identify and authenticate a token prefix, but they are not an inference prompt. A backend must obtain the actual token IDs before it can prefill the next model call. The vLLM capture path can send a TransferQueue staging chain to a generation worker because that worker can read the referenced rows. The Megatron Inference integration in Gym #2823 cannot do that today, so its capture handler sends required_prefix_token_ids inline.

    Backend pathCurrent prefix custody and deliveryCheckpoint consequence
    vLLM worker stagingThe worker stages each completed call in TransferQueue. Gym records a token-free staging chain. A child call sends that chain back to a worker, which fetches and verifies the prefix.The restored Gym ledger can continue referring to the restored TransferQueue rows. The worker needs no inline token array from Gym.
    Megatron Inference stagingThe merged baseline uses a finished-generation metadata ledger. In-flight NeMo-RL #3869 instead unifies Megatron and vLLM completed-call capture around Gym's CaptureAdmission and stages canonical records through the same TransferQueue sink before Gym records custody.That closes completed-call custody but not an active-generation cut. Before an in-flight checkpoint can publish, the engine must still detach the active Megatron prefix, stage it through the established sink, and give Gym the resulting durable coordinate.

    Make the delivery representation explicit

    prefix: InlinePrefix | StagedPrefix | None

InlinePrefix:
  kind: "inline"
  token_ids: [...]
  cumulative_hash: "..."

StagedPrefix:
  kind: "staged"
  staging_chain: [...]
  cumulative_hash: "..."

    A root call has no prefix. A child call has exactly one representation. An inline prefix carries exactly prev_len token IDs and no staging chain. A staged prefix carries a nonempty staging chain and no token array. Both retain the same parent_call_id, prev_len, parent chain hash, and cumulative token hash. This replaces the current implicit contract in CaptureAdmission, where required_prefix_token_ids and staging_chain are independent optional fields and can both be populated.

    Do not store both forms as competing custody records

    Persisting cumulative token arrays and a staging chain for the same prefix creates two possible sources of truth. The forms can disagree, and repeatedly storing the cumulative array makes storage grow quadratically across a long multi-turn rollout. The durable ledger should record one authoritative custody location. Prefix delivery can then adapt that location to the backend: vLLM dereferences a staged chain itself, while an RL-side prefix materializer can fetch the same chain and send inline tokens to Megatron Inference.

    Megatron checkpoint recovery needs more than the schema change

    The explicit prefix union is a localized wire-contract cleanup. Continuing an unfinished Megatron generation is a larger cross-repository change. Megatron Inference needs a cut operation for an active request rather than only completed-call capture. NeMo-RL #3869 puts completed Megatron and vLLM calls on the same durable staging path, which the active cut should reuse. During restore, either Megatron gains a TransferQueue prefix source or NeMo-RL materializes the staged prefix and sends it inline before prefill.

    Failure handling is fail-closed

    FailureObserved behaviorSafe next action
    A participant misses the prepare deadlineThe participant does not report a successful prepare. Agent status names executions still running, parked without a boundary, and completed without durable acknowledgement. Resources export raises instead of publishing a partial snapshot.Retire only an execution whose complete agent, model, and resources state can be discarded. Resources retirement waits for its mutation lock. Abort the global checkpoint when an external effect cannot be discarded safely.
    Model restore raisesModel admission stays paused and the control phase becomes restore_failed_paused. Capabilities and admission status expose that state.Retry the same restore or explicitly resume only when abandoning recovery is safe. Do not infer that a failed restore reopened traffic.
    A component commit failsNo valid manifest is published for that component. The server remains prepared and paused. A retry after a lost response validates and returns an already-published immutable manifest.Retry the same checkpoint ID or abort the global checkpoint. Never publish the controller checkpoint without every required component manifest.
    Restore finds a missing or corrupt fileDigest and schema validation fail before the replacement state becomes runnable. Resources restore requires a fresh process and activates the complete replacement set as one operation. Restored participants remain paused.Reject that checkpoint or demote the affected rollout to fresh dispatch only when the controller's global record permits that disposition.
    A request from attempt N arrives after restoring N+1Agent, model, and resources participants reject the request with 409 stale_attempt. Model-call roots from N remain tombstoned.Do not retry N. Route all resumed work through N+1.
    A FastAPI worker is missing during a multi-worker pauseThe coordinator cannot prove that service admission is closed or that the missing worker owns no accepted requests.Fail prepare. Never treat a missing worker as an in-flight count of zero.
    An agent reaches a terminal environment responseThe resources server retires the session, and the agent does not commit that terminal point as a resumable boundary.Use the completed result if NeMo-RL accepted it. Otherwise start a fresh attempt rather than stepping an already-terminal environment.

    Alternatives and their limits

    AlternativeWhat it simplifiesWhy it is not the general solution
    Restart every unfinished rolloutNo agent or resources checkpoint APIs. Only completed RL data and token rows need durability.It loses all progress in long multi-turn and SWE rollouts. It remains a valid fallback for stateless or unsupported environments and is the first milestone's recovery behavior.
    Wait for every rollout to finishThe checkpoint contains only terminal results, so no continuation state is needed.Checkpoint latency becomes the tail latency of the longest rollout. A hung tool or blackbox harness can block checkpoint publication indefinitely, which defeats periodic fault recovery.
    Replay the conversation and tool logAn append-only event log can be easier to inspect than snapshots.Replay is correct only when every effect is deterministic and idempotent. Judges, simulators, external APIs, clocks, random number generators, sandboxes, and failed requests can produce different state or duplicate effects. Replay is useful only for environments that explicitly prove those properties.
    Move all live state into NeMo-RL or one databaseA central service can take one database snapshot and expose one recovery API.It puts remote writes and a shared availability dependency on every agent turn and tool mutation. It also forces the controller to understand every agent, environment, and sandbox schema. Component ownership is lost, and the central schema becomes a bottleneck for new environments.
    Pull snapshots from each server without pausing admissionNo admission gates or drain protocol.The resulting files can describe different cuts. A processor boundary may reference an agent activation, resource mutation, or model call that committed after another component was copied. Digests prove file integrity, not cross-component consistency.
    Snapshot the whole process or containerOpaque agent memory and native library state can be preserved without application codecs.Process snapshots are provider- and kernel-specific and do not automatically make external HTTP calls, TransferQueue writes, sockets, or remote sandboxes consistent. This remains the likely extension for blackbox agents, paired with an egress relay and the same outer admission protocol.

    Why this approach fits Gym

    Gym already separates ownership across agent, model, and resources servers. The participant approach follows that boundary: shared infrastructure supplies identity, fencing, admission, manifest-last publication, and stale-attempt rejection, while each stateful implementation supplies only its codec and turn boundary. It preserves cheap drain-or-restart fallbacks, adds continuation one component at a time, and lets NeMo-RL coordinate the global checkpoint without importing environment-specific logic. The cost is more protocol surface and careful failure ordering. That cost is justified for expensive, long-running, stateful whitebox rollouts. Short stateless rollouts and opaque unsupported harnesses should continue to drain or restart.

    Assumptions the controller must enforce

    • Cross-component validation is an RL responsibility. The episode processor records last_committed_model_call_id, expected resources revisions, agent-session identity, and protocol position. Component manifests provide the corresponding model staging coordinates and private session state. Gym does not join them to a durable TransferQueue snapshot or choose the final recovery disposition.
    • The global commit marker is outside Gym. One Gym component can commit before another fails. The SingleController must select a checkpoint only after every required participant manifest validates.
    • Deadlines use synchronized wall clocks. Every request carries one absolute deadline_ts. Excessive clock skew can shorten or extend a participant's effective budget.
    • Only bounded waits enforce the deadline in the current stack. Prepare and model-drain paths consult deadline_ts. Component commit, restore, and resume still need explicit checks around potentially long filesystem or backend operations.
    • Checkpoint paths identify the same storage namespace. Server processes must see the controller-provided directory consistently. A remote or differently mounted worker cannot interpret a process-local path.
    • An unsuccessful mutation must not hide a committed effect. The resources middleware increments revisions only for successful HTTP responses. An environment that mutates state and then returns an error needs rollback or an explicit outcome record before it can claim continuation support.
    • Atomic resources activation is an environment callback contract. The shared participant passes the complete replacement set to restore_checkpoint_states. Each adapter must validate everything before replacing live maps; the framework cannot make a sequence of arbitrary environment mutations atomic on its own.
    • Completed results need a shared acknowledgement contract. The episode processor retains and reports completed-but-unacknowledged results, and retirement refuses to stand in for acknowledgement. NeMo-RL must durably accept the result before Gym can remove it from the recoverable live set. Component-session tombstone cleanup depends on the same ownership decision.
    • Capability discovery is necessary but not sufficient. A processor must commit a boundary after complete protocol operations, and each referenced stateful agent or resources session must implement its advertised snapshot contract. Inheriting checkpoint routes does not make a protocol resumable.

    APIs required to coordinate the checkpoint

    The checkpoint API is delivered in four additive milestones. Each milestone produces a useful recovery guarantee and becomes the foundation for the next one. Exists means the behavior is on the main branch. PR means the Gym checkpoint stack ending at #2946 or its linked NeMo-RL drafts contains the behavior. New means it still needs to be built.

    The SingleController calls the NemoGym actor. The actor calls Gym control endpoints. Episode processors call resources and agent session endpoints, and agents call model and tool endpoints while servicing /v1/responses. This keeps global checkpoint coordination out of protocol implementations while preserving component-owned state.

    Scope of the current Gym stack

    PRs #2939 through #2946 implement stable execution identity, response-egress and stale-attempt fences, exact worker-membership cuts, typed durable generation receipts, namespaced model-ledger commit and restore, receipt-bound agent completion acknowledgement, pending-model and turn-complete boundaries, exact-once resources mutation receipts, resources snapshots, initial stateful adapters, and the production-route end-to-end test in #2946. The experimental checkpoint modules are grouped under nemo_gym._checkpoint; no public Python import contract is claimed. NeMo-RL actor orchestration is in #4093. NeMo-RL already has native TransferQueue checkpointing and periodic rollout snapshots; adding Gym to that transaction, real inference-backend cuts, production multi-worker launcher wiring, and blackbox runtime snapshots remain outside these drafts.

    Milestone 1 — Preserve captured tokens for stateless rollouts

    This milestone supports direct-answer or otherwise restartable rollouts whose resources server and verifier retain no session state. It preserves exact token rows and their model-call lineage after they reach durable custody. It does not resume an episode processor, private agent session, or unfinished generation. A rollout that has not returned its result to NeMo-RL at the checkpoint boundary starts again from its original input after restore.

This milestone therefore excludes verifiers whose result must not be recomputed.
    Milestone 1 is not multi-turn continuationIt makes token capture and completed training data checkpoint-safe. It does not restore processor protocol state, private agent state, or a partially generated response.

    Milestone 2 — Resume an episode processor at a protocol boundary

    This milestone adds continuation for a whitebox episode protocol implemented inside Gym. Resources servers remain stateless in this milestone. The processor can therefore resume between resources seed, agent seed, agent activation, agent close, verification, resources close, and result return without requiring an environment snapshot.

    OwnerAdditional API or mechanismCheckpoint behavior
    Episode-processor baseprepare, checkpoint status, commit and restore, resume, and retire; one active /run per episode attempt.Prepare succeeds only when every tracked processor is parked with a committed EpisodeBoundaryRecord. Running work, a park without a boundary, or a completed result awaiting durable acknowledgement blocks publication.
    Episode protocol implementationCommit a typed boundary after each complete protocol operation. Record the next operation, open participant handles, completed inputs and outputs, cleanup obligations, and cross-component join fields.Restore creates attempt N+1, reconnects dependencies, and continues with the next operation without repeating a completed seed, activation, verification, or close.
    Agent-session participantExport and restore only private state behind agent_session_id: native continuation state, dependency descriptors, untransferred observations, and activation deduplication receipts.A stateless agent may have no payload. A stateful agent restores before the processor and rejects calls from attempt N.
    Checkpoint reconciliationJoin the processor boundary's last model-call ID, resources revision, and agent activation to restored model, resources, agent-session, and TransferQueue records.A missing or mismatched dependency downgrades only that rollout to fresh_dispatch; it never produces a continuation from an incomplete combination.

    Milestone 3 — Resume a whitebox agent with stateful resources

    This milestone adds logical environment-state recovery. It applies only to resources servers that can define a versioned session state and a safe concurrency contract. Accepted mutations drain before the server exports its frozen sessions.

    OwnerAdditional API or mechanismCheckpoint behavior
    Gym resources-server baseCheckpoint prepare, commit, restore, and resume; session registry keyed by (rollout_id, attempt); per-session mutation lock; stale-attempt rejection.No new mutation starts after prepare closes admission. Prepare waits for accepted mutations by acquiring each session lock, then exports the sessions that the process owns.
    Stateful environment implementationExplicit checkpoint_state_enabled opt-in plus versioned export_checkpoint_state, restore_checkpoint_states, and retire_checkpoint_state hooks.Restore validates and installs the complete logical state set under replacement attempts before any episode processor continuation becomes runnable.
    Nested model callsResources operations call dedicated auxiliary judge or simulator model instances rather than the paused policy instance.An accepted operation may finish its nested calls while policy-model admission is closed. The first implementation does not define admission leases.
    Deadline handlingdeadline_policy: restart_safe_rollouts plus a component capability declaring whether partial state can be discarded safely.A restart-safe session is fenced and discarded when its operation misses the deadline. Non-transactional external effects or shared mutable state abort the global checkpoint.

    Milestone 4 — Resume an opaque blackbox agent runtime

    This milestone comes last because Gym cannot ask an opaque harness to expose an operation boundary. Continuation requires checkpointing the process that owns the harness and controlling every request that can leave that process.

    OwnerAdditional API or mechanismCheckpoint behavior
    Runtime providerCapability negotiation for full_runtime_snapshot; freeze, checkpoint, restore-paused, resume, detach, and destroy; provider compatibility fingerprint.The snapshot includes the harness process tree and memory. Filesystem-only snapshots remain restart_only.
    Checkpoint-aware egress relayPause and resume forwarding; capture pending requests and cached responses; remap endpoints and attempt identity after restore.No request can escape the snapshotted runtime without appearing in relay state. An unfinished forwarded call is tombstoned and reissued under the replacement attempt.
    Blackbox-capable agent sessionAssociate the agent session with its runtime and relay descriptors; coordinate runtime freeze only after external calls drain or are classified for reissue.Restore reconnects the runtime, relay, model lineage, resources state, and agent session before the episode processor resumes.

    The completed audit has an issue-backed disposition for every server

    The audit was reconciled against the then-current upstream/main and accounts for 121 resources-server directories and 47 agent directories. #3024 — Partial rollout checkpointing for long-running Gym executions is the umbrella. Its first-level issues separate generation cuts, logical resources state, whitebox agents, opaque runtimes, sandbox state, coordinated or drain-only services, inference engines, and training frameworks.

    Issues record work; they do not prove supportEvery child listed below is open implementation or validation work unless this section explicitly marks the adapter implemented. A server with no child is still required to advertise and satisfy its audited capability before checkpointing is enabled.

    The whitebox audit now has two questions

    For each protocol, determine what the episode processor must retain to choose its next operation. Separately, determine whether the selected agent server has private state behind agent_session_id. A processor can be resumable while using a stateless agent, and a stateful or opaque agent session can force an otherwise simple processor to restart. Existing whitebox-agent issues should be reclassified along this boundary instead of assuming that every agent owns its complete episode loop.

    Implemented adapters that do not need new issues

    blackjack, example_session_state_mgmt, and workplace_assistant already have resources-state adapters in the draft stack. The GymnasiumServer base also has shared resources hooks. The existing simple_agent and gymnasium_agent continuation changes prove useful state fields, but their protocol position must move into episode processors. Only private state that remains inside their seeded agent sessions should stay in agent-side adapters. labbench2_vlm_agent inherits the SimpleAgent behavior and should follow the same split.

    Explicit restart-only agents without continuation children

    non_executing_simple_agent, tool_simulation_agent, and verifiers_agent intentionally have no per-agent continuation issue. Their advertised behavior must remain restart-only unless a later design proves a valid continuation boundary.

    Resources servers that need no adapter issue

    These resources servers are stateless for checkpointing or can safely reconstruct their local state. This classification means that no server-specific export/restore adapter is planned. It does not make an unfinished rollout resumable, and it does not remove the need for explicit capability reporting.
